issue_context.title: Failed to start Store a SystemToken in an EFI Variable
issue_context.body:
**systemd version the issue has been seen with**
> 243.0

**Used distribution**
 > Archlinux

**Expected behaviour you didn't see**
 > With random seed successfully already set in EFI variable through `#bootctl random-seed`, systemd-boot-system-token.service should not fire.

**Unexpected behaviour you saw**
 > Unit started and failed with error:
`Failed to start Store a System Token in an EFI Variable`

**Steps to reproduce the problem**
> Start systemd-boot-system-token.service with default
`ConditionPathExists=|!/sys/firmware/efi/efivars/LoaderRandomSeed-4a67b082-0a4c-41cf-b6c7-440b29bb8c4f`
No such file exists even with EFI variable already set through `#bootctl random-seed`.
Suspect the EFI variable's name changed?  No error when unit file amended to:
`ConditionPathExists=|!/sys/firmware/efi/efivars/LoaderSystemToken-4a67b082-0a4c-41cf-b6c7-440b29bb8c4f`

So this bug report is not very useful anymore, since multiple people have multiple different problems, and things are really not as related as people think. i.e. EROFS is very different from EINVAL, which in turn is very different from the ESP not found issue.

Either way, I have now prepared #14083, which should make these EINVAL and the ESP not found issue go away. The EROFS issue was a local misconfiguration and we should really ignore hence.

As soon as #14083 is merged this issues is closed. If there are issues remaining even then, please open up new issues, and let *us* merge them when we deem them the same problem, to keep the noise down.

Anyway, it would be great if people who ran into the EINVAL or "ESP not found" issue to test #14083 please. Everyone else please don't bother, it's not going to fix the issue for you anyway, and please refrain from commenting to keep the noise level minimal, thank you.

#14083 is a bit of a chickening out. The EINVAL issue is an error propagated from the EFI firmware, which refuses to write our EFI variable. It might be worth tracking down why or under which conditions that happens specifically, but since I don't have your hardware/firmware I cannot test this myself. For example, the EFI variable value we write is 512 bytes long (which is relatively large I guess), it might be worth exploring if maybe smaller variables would work. Also, we write a binary blob, and it might be worth exploring if NUL terminating or base64 encoding or UTF-16 reencoding might help on those firmwares. Hence, if anyone is technically savvy enough to play around with the C code, it would be very welcome to hear back which variables can be written and which ones can't, and maybe we can rework our code to so that it works on your firmware too.

Either way, the PR should make the error go away for all cases, so if you have a firmware allergic to these kind of EFI variables it's fine, we'll just skip over it and not complain (though of course you won't get pre-boot random seed initialization that way either).

Got a similar problem, which I realize is for a new issue, but wanted to document the workaround that is available nowadays.

My `ASUS MAXIMUS VII HERO` throws up a `Failed to write 'LoaderSystemToken' EFI variable: Invalid argument` during install.

However, since https://github.com/pdmorrow/systemd/commit/41d22841ce996eee7c6fd87c029d39248ea0d8f9 one can use the `--graceful` flag to ignore the problem and continue with the installation.

```bash
# bootctl install --graceful
...
Unable to write 'LoaderSystemToken' EFI variable (firmware problem?), ignoring: Invalid argument
...
```

review_comments: That seems wrong. If I call `bootctl random-seed` I really expect something to happen and we shouldn't suppress errors. If the service that uses that command is called in wrong conditions, then the conditionalization of the service needs to be fixed.

The conditionalization is really hard, since the ESP might be mounted at a variety of places really. we actively search for it. Note that you will still see a log msg if we skip operation, so it's not that it's entirely silent and invisible...

Then I think we need to check if we are running as part of the service, and only change behaviour in that case. I think making this explicit would be best: add a command line option `--skip-if-no-efi`, and call `bootctl random-seed --skip-if-no-efi` in the unit.
